'''Roy Jay Glauber''' (September 1, 1925 – December 26, 2018) was an American [[theoretical physicist]]. He was the [[Mallinckrodt]] [[Professor]] of [[Physics]] at [[Harvard University]] and Adjunct Professor of Optical Sciences at the [[University of Arizona]]. Born in New York City, he was awarded one half of the 2005 [[Nobel Prize in Physics]] "for his contribution to the quantum theory of [[Coherence (physics)|optical coherence]]", with the other half shared by [[John L. Hall]] and [[Theodor W. Hänsch]]. In this work, published in 1963, he created a model for [[photodetection]] and explained the fundamental characteristics of different types of light, such as [[laser]] light (see [[coherent state]]) and light from light bulbs (see [[blackbody]]). His theories are widely used in the field of [[quantum optics]].<ref name="Glauber2009">{{cite journal |last1=Glauber |first1=Roy |title=An interview with Nobel laureate Roy Glauber, Physics 2005 |journal=Journal of Visualized Experiments |issue=28 |pages=1535 |year=2009 |issn=1940-087X |doi=10.3791/1535 |pmid=19561567 |pmc=3149897}}</ref><ref>R. J. Glauber, ''Quantum Theory of Optical Coherence. Selected Papers and Lectures'', Wiley-VCH, Weinheim 2007. (A collection of reprints of Glauber's most important papers from 1963 to 1999, selected by the author.)</ref> In [[statistical physics]] he pioneered the study of the dynamics of first-order [[phase transitions]], since he first defined and investigated the [[stochastic]] dynamics of an [[Ising model]] in a paper published in 1963.<ref name="GlauberJMP1963">{{cite journal|last1=Glauber|first1=R.J.|title=Time-dependent statistics of the Ising model|journal=Journal of Mathematical Physics|volume=4|issue=2|pages=294–307|year=1963|doi=10.1063/1.1703954|bibcode=1963JMP.....4..294G}}</ref>  

He served on the National Advisory Board of the Center for Arms Control and Non-Proliferation, the research arm of [[Council for a Livable World]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Board Members |url=https://armscontrolcenter.org/about/board/#RGlauber |website=Center for Arms Control and Non-Proliferation |access-date=22 September 2016}}</ref> 

==Education==
Glauber was born in 1925 in New York City the son of Felicia (Fox) and Emanuel B. Glauber.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=CZNNAQAAIAAJ&q=%22Emanuel+B.+and+Felicia+(Fox)+G.%22 |title=World Who's who in Science: A Biographical Dictionary of Notable Scientists from Antiquity to the Present |first=Allen G. |last=Debus |date=6 January 1968 |publisher=Marquis-Who's Who |via=Google Books}}</ref> He was a member of the 1941 graduating class of the [[Bronx High School of Science]], the first graduating class from that school.  He then did his undergraduate work at [[Harvard University]]. 

After his sophomore year, he was recruited to work on the [[Manhattan Project]], where (at the age of 18) he was one of the youngest scientists at [[Los Alamos National Laboratory]]. His work involved calculating the [[critical mass]] for the [[atom bomb]]. After two years at Los Alamos, he returned to Harvard, receiving his bachelor's degree in 1946 and his PhD in 1949.<ref name=phd>{{cite thesis |degree=PhD |first=Roy Jay|last=Glauber |title=The relativistic theory of meson fields |publisher=[[Harvard University]] |date=1949 |bibcode=1949PhDT.........7G |oclc=76985581}}</ref>

==Research==
Glauber's research dealt with problems in a number of areas of quantum optics, a field which, broadly speaking, studies the [[quantum electrodynamic]]al interactions of light and matter. He also continued work on several topics in high-energy collision theory, including the analysis of [[hadron]] collisions, and the [[Glauber multiple scattering theory|statistical correlation of particles produced in high-energy reactions]].<ref name="Glauber:1963fi">
{{cite journal
 |last1=Glauber |first1=R.J.
 |title=High energy collision theory.
 |journal=Brittin WE, Dunham LG, Eds. Lectures in Theoretical Physics, Volume I. Wiley-Interscience
 |year=1959
 |url=https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.177153
 }}</ref><ref name="Glauber:1970wr">
{{cite book
 |last1=Glauber |first1=R.J.
 |title=High-Energy Physics and Nuclear Structure
 |chapter=Theory of High Energy Hadron-Nucleus Collisions
 |year=1970
 |pages=207–264
 |doi=10.1007/978-1-4684-1827-9_43
 |isbn=978-1-4684-1829-3
 }}</ref><ref>
{{cite journal
 |last1=Bauer |first1=T. H.
 |last2=Spital |first2=R. D.
 |last3= Yennie |first3= D.R..
 |last4=Pipkin |first4=F. M.
 |title=The Hadronic Properties of the Photon in High-Energy Interactions
 |journal=Reviews of Modern Physics
 |volume=50
 |year=1978
 |issue=2
 |page=261
 |doi=10.1103/RevModPhys.50.261
 |bibcode=1978RvMP...50..261B
 }}</ref>

Roy Glauber’s early work on multiple scattering theory started in the 1950s and was continued with his students, such as Victor Franco.<ref>{{cite journal | url=https://journals.aps.org/pr/abstract/10.1103/PhysRev.142.1195 | doi=10.1103/PhysRev.142.1195 | title=High-Energy Deuteron Cross Sections | date=1966 | last1=Franco | first1=V. | last2=Glauber | first2=R. J. | journal=Physical Review | volume=142 | issue=4 | pages=1195–1214 | bibcode=1966PhRv..142.1195F }}</ref>

Specific topics of his research included: the quantum mechanical behavior of trapped [[wave packet]]s; interactions of light with trapped ions; atom counting-the statistical properties of free atom beams and their measurement; algebraic methods for dealing with [[fermion]] statistics; coherence and correlations of [[bosonic atom]]s near the [[Bose–Einstein condensation]]; the theory of continuously monitored photon counting-and its reaction on quantum sources; the fundamental nature of "[[Atomic electron transition|quantum jumps]]"; resonant transport of particles produced multiply in high-energy collisions; the multiple diffraction model of proton-proton and proton-antiproton scattering.{{citationneeded|date=November 2022}}

==Awards and honors==
Glauber received the [[Albert A. Michelson Medal]] from the [[Franklin Institute]] in [[Philadelphia]] (1985),<ref name="MichelsonMedal_Laureates">{{cite web |url=https://www.fi.edu/laureates/roy-j-glauber |title=Roy J. Glauber, Physics (1985) |date=15 January 2014 |publisher=[[Franklin Institute]] |access-date=June 29, 2022 }}</ref> the Max Born Award from the [[Optical Society of America]] (1985), the [[Dannie Heineman Prize for Mathematical Physics]] from the [[American Physical Society]] (1996), and shared the 2005 [[Nobel Prize in Physics]]. Glauber was awarded the 'Medalla de Oro del [[Spanish National Research Council|CSIC]]' ('CSIC's Gold Medal') in a ceremony held in [[Madrid, Spain]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.csic.es/documentos/destacados/medalla_csic08.pdf |title=Nota informativa acto de entrega de la medalla de Oro del CSIC al profesor Roy J. Glauber |access-date=2008-04-23 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080530175716/http://www.csic.es/documentos/destacados/medalla_csic08.pdf <!-- Bot retrieved archive --> |archive-date = 2008-05-30}}</ref> He was elected a [[List of Fellows of the Royal Society elected in 1997|Foreign Member of the Royal Society (ForMemRS) in 1997]].<ref name=frs>{{cite web |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150316060617/https://royalsociety.org/about-us/fellowship/fellows/ |archive-date=2015-03-16 |url=https://royalsociety.org/about-us/fellowship/fellows/ |publisher=[[Royal Society]] |location=London |title=Fellows of the Royal Society}}</ref>

Glauber was awarded half the 2005 Nobel prize, along with experimentalists [[John L. Hall|John Hall]] and [[Theodor W. Hänsch|Theodor Hänsch]], recognized for their work on precision spectroscopy.<ref name="NYTobit">{{Cite news |date=2019-01-08 |title=Roy J. Glauber, 93, Dies; Nobel Laureate Explored Behavior of Light |work=The New York Times |language=en |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/01/08/obituaries/roy-j-glauber-dead.html |access-date=2023-08-14 |last1=McClain |first1=Dylan Loeb }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Nobel Doubts |url=https://www.insidehighered.com/news/2005/12/07/nobel-doubts |access-date=2022-11-30 |website=www.insidehighered.com |language=en}}</ref>

===Ig Nobel===
For many years before winning his Nobel Prize, Glauber took part in the [[Ig Nobel Prize]] ceremonies, where he appeared each year as "Keeper of the Broom," sweeping the stage clean of the [[paper airplane]]s that have traditionally been thrown during the event.  He missed the 2005 event as he was being awarded the Nobel Prize for Physics.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Abrahams |first=Marc |date=2018-12-28 |title=Sad news: Roy Glauber, paper airplane sweeper and physicist of light, is gone |url=https://improbable.com/2018/12/27/sad-news-roy-glauber-paper-airplane-sweeper-and-physicist-of-light-is-gone/ |access-date=2023-08-14 |website=improbable.com |language=en-US}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Glauber's father was a traveling salesman. When Glauber was six years of age, his mother gave birth to his sister, and the family settled in the New York City area. Glauber was very interested in astronomy as a child. In December 1937, along with several other children, he gave a presentation at the [[American Museum of Natural History]] in New York City, about a reflecting telescope he had built on his own. The assistant to the director of the [[Hayden Planetarium]], Dorothy Bennett, was present; she was a lecturer at the planetarium. Bennett was impressed with Glauber's work and she encouraged his membership and subsequent activity in an extra-curricular group for astronomy for the next few years. Glauber said she was "an influence in my life" and "a truly extraordinary spirit".  After his work at Los Alamos, he visited her at her home, as she had moved to Taos, New Mexico.<ref name="AHF2013">{{cite web |last1=Kelly |first1=Cindy |title=Roy Glauber's Interview (2013) - Nuclear Museum |url=https://ahf.nuclearmuseum.org/voices/oral-histories/roy-glaubers-interview-2013/ |website=Voices of the Manhattan Project |publisher=[[Atomic Heritage Foundation]] |access-date=8 March 2025 |location=Cambridge, Massachusetts |date=6 June 2013}}</ref>

Glauber lived in [[Arlington, Massachusetts]]. He was a guest scientist at the [[CERN|European Organization for Nuclear Research (CERN)]] in 1967, during a sabbatical.<ref name="nobelBio">{{cite web |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2005/glauber/biographical/ |title=Roy J. Glauber - Biographical |publisher=The Nobel Prize |first=Roy J. |last=Glauber |access-date=2019-07-12}}</ref> In 1951, he became a temporary lecturer at the [[California Institute of Technology]], where he replaced [[Richard Feynman]].<ref name="nobelBio" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Glauber, Roy J., 1925- |url=https://history.aip.org/phn/11511010.html |access-date=2022-08-11 |website=history.aip.org}}</ref>

Glauber had a son and a daughter, and five grandchildren. He died on December 26, 2018, in [[Newton, Massachusetts]].<ref>{{cite news |first=Martin |last=Weil |title=Roy Glauber, Nobel-winning physicist who applied quantum mechanics to optics, dies at 93 |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/obituaries/roy-glauber-nobel-winning-physicist-who-applied-quantum-mechanics-to-optics-dies-at-93/2018/12/30/b7e4e05e-0b24-11e9-a3f0-71c95106d96a_story.html |newspaper=The Washington Post |date=December 30, 2018 |access-date=September 12, 2019}}</ref>  He was one of the last surviving witnesses to the [[Trinity (nuclear test)|Trinity nuclear test]].<ref>{{cite web | url=https://english.elpais.com/science-tech/2022-04-26/roy-glauber-the-last-witness-to-the-manhattan-project.html |title=Roy Glauber: The last witness to the Manhattan Project |date=27 April 2022 }}</ref>  He was buried in [[Kensico Cemetery]], [[Valhalla, New York]].<ref name="NYTobit" /><ref>{{cite web |title=In Memoriam: Roy J. Glauber, 1925-2018 |url=https://www.osa.org/en-us/about_osa/newsroom/obituaries/roy_j_glauber/ |access-date=28 December 2018}}</ref>

==Memoirs==
A book by quantum physicist {{ill|José Ignacio Latorre|es}} and M.T. Soto-Sanfiel contains Roy J. Glauber's memoirs of the Manhattan Project and aspects of his scientific and personal life, based on a series of interviews conducted in Singapore, Spain, and the U.S. It has been published in English<ref>{{cite book |last1=Latorre |first1=José Ignacio |last2=Soto-Sanfiel |first2=María Teresa |title=The Last Voice: Roy J. Glauber and the Dawn of the Atomic Age |date=2023 |doi=10.1007/978-3-031-29984-1 |isbn=978-3-031-29983-4 |url=https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-031-29984-1 |access-date=9 March 2025 |language=en}}</ref> and Spanish.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Latorre |first1=José Ignacio |last2=Soto-Sanfiel |first2=María Teresa |title=La última voz: Roy J. Glauber y el inicio de la era atómica |date=2022 |id={{ASIN|8434435233|country=sg}} |language=es}}</ref>  The same authors produced a documentary of the same name, "That's the Story: Roy J. Glauber Remembers the Making of the Atomic Bomb" featuring Glauber recounting some of his experiences within the Manhattan Project <ref>url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=l1KfERVRjos |access-date=25 April 2025</ref>
